meta.name: Primordial Paradox drum pattern library
meta.author: research-assistant
meta.purpose: Give the arranger a measured, sourced vocabulary of NES drum grooves and fills, with the waltz written as a family rather than one pattern, because the ear review of title theme v3 scored the drums 4 of 10 and blamed a waltz that never changed.
meta.method: Technique read from public chip documentation and drum tutorials (DR-S01 to DR-S10), mapped onto this project's renderer (DR-S11), then written as original grids. No copyrighted pattern was copied or transcribed; the two plain control patterns are written here from the same technique as everything else.

grid_legend.steps: one bar of 16 steps in 4/4, one bar of 12 steps in 3/4, two bars of 6 eighth steps in 6/8, each step one subdivision (16th, 16th, 8th)
grid_legend.step: a list of hits; a step may hold a noise hit and a DMC hit together because they are separate channels
grid_legend.accent: true when velocity is 113 or more, which is authoring level 8 or 9
grid_legend.period: noise timer period 0 to 15; higher is darker and slower, so a rising period across hits is a falling pitch
grid_legend.loop: long is white noise, short is the 93 step metallic buzz
grid_legend.rate: DMC playback rate index 0 to 15; higher is brighter and shorter

meta.statistics_dependency: The MUS-DATA-STATS card's corpus statistics were not on disk when this file was written (no data/*stats*.json), so every rule here comes from the public sources listed below plus this project's own renderer. When the stats json lands, the counts to compare against are the accent positions and the bar lengths in this file's patterns.

sources.title: NESdev Wiki, APU Noise
sources.claim: The noise channel has 16 timer periods, from 4 CPU cycles ($0) to 4068 ($F) NTSC. The mode flag picks feedback bit 6 (a 93 step or 31 step buzzy sequence) instead of bit 1 (the 32767 step white sequence). The period table gives the repeat rate for each value, so period 0 is a 4811 Hz hiss and period F is a 4.7 Hz flutter.

sources.title: NESdev Wiki, APU DMC
sources.claim: The DMC plays 1 bit delta samples at 16 playback rates ($4010 low nibble), 4181 Hz at $0 up to 33143 Hz at $F. A one byte loop gives a pitched buzz, a 17 byte loop gives mid pitches, a 33 byte loop gives very low pitches, which is how a short sample becomes a drum.

sources.title: NESdev Wiki, APU Envelope
sources.claim: Every channel has a constant volume mode with 16 levels and a decaying envelope with 16 divider periods plus a loop flag. Volume is close to linear, so a velocity ramp from the tracker reads as a smooth crescendo.

sources.title: Ripples Music, How to make 8 bit drums without a sample pack
sources.claim: A chip kit is noise with a fast envelope for hats and snares plus a fast falling tone for kicks and toms. Closed hat decay is 20 to 40 ms, open hat 150 to 250 ms, snare body 120 to 180 ms, kick pitch fall about 30 ms. Varying the decay rather than the volume is the expressive control, and the NES had one noise channel plus whatever the triangle was not using.

sources.title: Soundbrenner, Hemiola
sources.claim: Six equal subdivisions can be heard as two groups of three or three groups of two. In 3/4 a hemiola stretches across two bars, so the accents fall every two quarter notes and there are three larger pulses in the space of two bars.

sources.title: Music Stack Exchange, What is it called when 2/2 is imposed in 3/4
sources.claim: A hemiola needs the metre of three established first, then the pattern of two set against it; a two against three that is never anchored sounds like a metre change instead of a hemiola.

sources.title: Music Production Wiki, How to recreate the chiptune sound
sources.claim: The noise channel offers sixteen preset frequencies and its own volume envelope. A fast attack and instant decay is a hi hat, a longer decay at a lower noise pitch is a snare, and the short mode gives the tonal metallic buzz. The DMC let later composers stream real drum hits, which is why late NES kits are punchier than early ones.

sources.title: jfound, How to make chiptune music in your browser
sources.claim: A 16 step grid with kick on 1 and 9, a short noise hit on 5 and 13 for the snare, and hats for constant motion is the canonical starting groove, and a single noise channel can only hold one sound at a time, so busy layered programming breaks the illusion.

sources.title: Frontiers in Psychology 5:1257, Neural correlates of intentional switching from ternary to binary meter in a musical hemiola pattern
sources.claim: Accent strength at each pulse position is modelled for binary (march), ternary (waltz) and hemiola patterns. Downbeats carry several coinciding metric layers and upbeats only one, and in a hemiola the positions where three layers coincide are the strongest and act as the pivot for a metre switch.

sources.title: Alexander Brandon, 8 bit music: a practical guide
sources.claim: Program the noise channel as drums: short bursts are hi hats, longer ones are snares, and pitch and length are the only controls. Percussion carries the groove in chiptune because there is nothing else to carry it.

sources.title: This repository, tools/render_chip.py
sources.claim: The project renderer maps a noise note to period index pitch - 1 clamped to 0..15, plays the short mode when CC12 has bit 0 set, renders DMC kick on MIDI note 36 and DMC snare on note 38, and applies a per note linear decay. So a noise period p is written as MIDI note p + 1 and a short mode hit needs CC12 = 1 at that note.

noise.chip: 2A03 noise channel ($400C volume, $400E period and mode, $400F length)

period_usage.0-2: closed hat, tick, brightest hiss (4811 to 1202 Hz repeat)
period_usage.3-5: open hat, rim, short snare top
period_usage.14-15: sub thump, cymbal wash, longest decay

loop_mode.long: 32767 step white noise, the normal drum and hat sound
loop_mode.short: 93 or 31 step metallic buzz, for cymbals, robots and ghost tails

noise.renderer_mapping: period p -> MIDI note p + 1; loop short -> CC12 = 1 on that note; note length is the decay

dpcm_kick.chip: DMC ($4010 rate, $4011 direct load, $4012 address, $4013 length)
dpcm_kick.renderer_mapping: MIDI note 36, velocity is the accent

dpcm_snare.chip: DMC, a 17 to 33 byte noise loop
dpcm_snare.renderer_mapping: MIDI note 38, velocity is the accent

waltz.channel_budget: noise plus DMC; the triangle is usually busy with the bass in 3/4
waltz.rule: The waltz tread is one bar of three; the drum writing lives in which of the three beats carries weight, not in how many hits there are.

march.channel_budget: DMC kick and snare, noise for ruffs
march.rule: A march is a snare part first and a kit second: the side drum states the rudiments and the bass drum marks the floor.

rock.channel_budget: DMC kick, DMC snare, noise hat
rock.rule: Backbeat on 2 and 4, eighth or sixteenth hat, and one displaced kick per bar. The displaced kick is what separates rock from four on the floor.

metal.channel_budget: DMC kick as a wall, DMC snare as the backbeat, noise hat
metal.rule: The kick is the riff. Any bar where the kick stops is a bar the guitar has to carry alone, so stop it deliberately and never by accident.

baroque.channel_budget: DMC timpani, noise only as a shadow
baroque.rule: Accents only. A baroque texture puts the drums on the metre and the continuo carries the motion, so a rock hat pattern destroys the style instantly.

boss.channel_budget: DMC kick low rate, DMC snare, noise tom
boss.rule: Asymmetry and space. The boss groove avoids a repeating two bar cell inside one bar, because the player should not be able to predict the next hit.

calm.channel_budget: noise at high period, one soft DMC kick
calm.rule: Levels at 2 or 3 and periods at 7 or higher. Calm is a level and period decision, not a rhythm decision.

battle.channel_budget: DMC kick and snare, noise hat; the pulse channels belong to the lead
battle.rule: The drums hold the tempo and nothing else, because the lead is doing the work. Every battle pattern must survive being played under a lead at sixteenth density.

patterns.name: Plain boom chick chick (control case)
patterns.note: The pattern the ear review heard for 52 bars. Kick on 1, one noise stab on 2 and 3. Every other waltz pattern here exists to replace it.

patterns.name: Hemiola bar A: accents on 1 and 3
patterns.note: Paired with WZ-03. Two bars of this and WZ-03 put heavy accents on 1, 3, then 2, which is the classic two bars of 3/4 heard as three beats of 2/4 (DR-S05).

patterns.name: Hemiola bar B: accent pulled to beat 2
patterns.note: The other half of the hemiola pair. Alternate WZ-02 and WZ-03 for two bar hemiola cells.

patterns.name: Hemiola pivot on the shared accent
patterns.note: Duple grouping inside one bar: 0 and 6 are six steps apart and land on the half bar points the ear starts counting in twos, then 10 breaks the expectation.

patterns.name: Vertical hemiola: noise in twos over kick in threes
patterns.note: Both groupings at once: the kick states three beats, the hat and snare accents every third sixteenth group. Brahms used this two against three layering (DR-S06).

patterns.name: Kick on 1 and the and of 2
patterns.note: The second kick sits on the and of 2 instead of beat 3. This is the single cheapest cure for a stiff waltz: the bar stops being a clock.

patterns.name: Kick on 1 and the and of 2, ghost snare after
patterns.note: Kick pushes the bar forward, snare answers on 3, ghost on the a of 3 keeps the motion alive into the next bar.

patterns.name: Kick on 1, and of 2, and the and of 3
patterns.note: Three kicks with no two in the same place. Use once per eight bars at most, or the surprise becomes the rule.

patterns.name: Kick on 1 and 2 and, snare late
patterns.note: A sixteenth early on beat 2 (step 5) reads as a small push, softer than WZ-06 but it does the same job.

patterns.name: Snare on 3 with three ghosts
patterns.note: Ghosts at levels 2 to 3 are about 28 to 42 velocity, which on the chip reads as the noise envelope tail rather than a second snare. Level 3 is the ceiling for a ghost.

patterns.name: Snare on 3, ghost flam before it
patterns.note: A flam written as two hits 1 step apart, the soft one first. On the chip a one step flam at 100 bpm is about 60 ms apart, which is the range where a flam reads as one thick hit.

patterns.name: Snare on 3, brushed ghosts, low and short
patterns.note: Period 6 for the ghosts makes them read brushed instead of sharp, and it is quiet enough that the ghost pattern survives a phone speaker.

patterns.name: Snare on 3 with buzz ghosts in short mode
patterns.note: Short loop mode turns the ghost tail into the metallic buzz the 93 step sequence gives (DR-S01), so the quiet hits sit in a different texture from the snare.

patterns.name: March waltz: even eighths, snare on 3
patterns.note: The waltz played as a march in three: steady eighths in the hat, bass drum on 1 and 2, snare on 3. A march pulse disguises the boom chick chick without changing the harmony.

patterns.name: March waltz with a rudimental ruff
patterns.note: Ruff into beat 3, then two taps after it. This is the one bar of a four bar phrase where a march waltz is allowed to speak.

patterns.name: March waltz, snare drum carries the beat
patterns.note: Snare on 2 and 3, kick only on 1. Reads as a side drum part rather than a kit, which is the right register for a title screen.

patterns.name: Rock waltz: backbeat on 3, kick on 1 and the and of 2
patterns.note: Eighth hat, kick on 1 and the and of 2, snare on 3 as the backbeat. At 120 bpm and up this is a rock groove that happens to be in three.

patterns.name: Rock waltz with an open hat on 2
patterns.note: A low period number is a brighter hiss, so the open hat is written as period 9 at moderate velocity, which the renderer decays over the note length.

patterns.name: Rock waltz, half time
patterns.note: One kick, one snare, three quiet hats. The space is the point: it leaves room for the lead and it makes WZ-17 sound loud when it returns.

patterns.name: Rock waltz with sixteenth pickup
patterns.note: The sixteenth pickup at 11 and the early kick at 6 are what make the bar lean into the next one.

patterns.name: Baroque pulse: three equal accents, nothing else
patterns.note: One instrument, three evenly weighted accents. No filler at all: this is how a dance suite states a metre when the harmony is doing the moving.

patterns.name: Baroque pulse: 1 heavy, 2 and 3 light
patterns.note: The accent hierarchy the metre implies: downbeat heavy, other beats left at level 4, which is about 57 velocity on the chip ramp.

patterns.name: Baroque timpani: root on 1, fifth on 3
patterns.note: Two pitches, spelled as two DMC rates rather than two samples: rate 10 for the low stroke, rate 12 for the higher one, which is the cheapest timpani the chip can do.

patterns.name: Baroque cadential hemiola
patterns.note: The written out ritardando the baroque hemiola is: two bars of three become three of two as the phrase cadences (DR-S05). Use it in the two bars before a section change, not inside one.

patterns.name: Cut time feel: two pulses, kick on 1 and 3
patterns.note: Three quarter notes but two felt pulses: kick and snare alternate 1, 2, 3 and the bar reads as a slow two. Written as 3/4 so the harmony still moves in threes.

patterns.name: Cut time feel: dotted quarter hats
patterns.note: Hats land on a dotted quarter grid (steps 4 and 9), which pulls the bar across the beat instead of sitting on it.

patterns.name: Cut time into hemiola pivot
patterns.note: Starts as a two pulse bar and the hits at 4 and 10 tilt it back towards three. A one bar ambiguity is the safest dose of hemiola.

patterns.name: Drop out bar: hat only on 2 and 3
patterns.note: The no kick bar of the variation ladder. One bar of this every eight bars resets the ear, and it costs no channel at all.

patterns.name: Waltz with DMC kick flam and rim
patterns.note: Kick flam on the downbeat, rim on 2, snare on 3. A double hit on the downbeat is what makes a waltz sound played rather than programmed.

patterns.name: Compound waltz: two big beats, six eight notes
patterns.note: In 6/8 the tread is two dotted quarters per bar, so the snare lands inside the beat (step 3 and 9) rather than on it. Twelve steps cover two bars.

patterns.name: Compound waltz with three against two
patterns.note: Three kicks across six eighths, which is the 3/4 reading of a 6/8 bar. Bernstein's America does exactly this swap (DR-S06).

patterns.name: Compound waltz, siciliana lilt
patterns.note: Sparse and slow: the dotted rhythm is in the melody, so the drums only mark the two big beats and the second eighth of each.

patterns.name: Compound waltz, cut rate drums
patterns.note: The 6/8 groove played fast enough to read as a rock waltz. Tempo does most of the stylistic work here.

patterns.name: Compound waltz with a two bar answer
patterns.note: Bar one states, bar two answers a step earlier. Two bars is the smallest unit where a compound groove can say something and reply to itself.

patterns.name: Compound waltz, drums drop out for bar two
patterns.note: One bar of groove, one bar of almost nothing. This is the ladder's drop out rung in compound metre.

patterns.name: March: kick 1 and 3, snare 2 and 4
patterns.note: The plain march. Everything else in this feel is this pattern with one element changed.

patterns.name: March: eight note snare rudiment
patterns.note: Soft taps before each main snare hit, the way a marching snare plays a ruff into the beat.

patterns.name: March: sixteenth snare roll on beat 4
patterns.note: The last beat is already a fill, so this pattern can run into a section change without a separate fill bar.

patterns.name: March: bass drum only on 1
patterns.note: One kick per bar makes the snare the lead voice, which is what a side drum march sounds like when the band is walking.

patterns.name: March: dotted pickup on the and of 4
patterns.note: The snare pickup at 14 and 15 pushes into the next bar instead of stopping on beat 4.

patterns.name: March: two bar press roll
patterns.note: Alternating soft and medium sixteenths read as a press roll. On the chip the illusion needs the levels to stay uneven, so the grid is written with two levels.

patterns.name: March: 6/8 compound march
patterns.note: Two bars of 6/8: the snare answers inside each big beat instead of on it.

patterns.name: March: cut time two feel
patterns.note: Same skeleton, quieter hats and softer backbeats, so the bar reads as two slow beats rather than four.

patterns.name: March: snare stops, kick carries
patterns.note: No snare at all for one bar. A march without its side drum sounds like held breath, which is exactly what a bar before a section needs.

patterns.name: March: triplet feel on beats 2 and 4
patterns.note: A sixteenth grid cannot hold a true triplet, so the gesture is written as main hit plus two softer hits inside the next two steps, which the ear rounds to a triplet at march tempo.

patterns.name: March: crescendo by level only
patterns.note: A single bar that gets louder without adding notes. The NES envelope is linear in volume, so the ramp reads cleanly.

patterns.name: March: cadence roll on the last beat
patterns.note: The roll ends on the loudest hit of the bar, which is the hit that lands on the downbeat of the next section.

patterns.name: March: snare and kick in unison (tutti)
patterns.note: Kick and snare together on every beat, which is how a chip fakes a band hitting the same step at once.

patterns.name: March: ghost sixteenths under everything
patterns.note: Weak sixteenths between the eighths at level 2. It fills the bar without adding a voice, because the noise channel was idle on those steps anyway.

patterns.name: March: spare and halting
patterns.note: A march with holes in it. Useful when the melody is march-like but the mood is not triumphant.

patterns.name: Rock: kick 1 and 3, snare 2 and 4, eighth hats
patterns.note: The reference rock groove. Every other pattern in this feel is a decision about which of these three layers to move.

patterns.name: Rock: sixteenth hats
patterns.note: Sixteenth hats with accents on the eighths. The accented steps are the ones the ear counts, so the sixteenths read as motion rather than as speed.

patterns.name: Rock: half time
patterns.note: The backbeat moves from 4 and 12 to 8 alone. Half time doubles the felt space without changing the tempo line.

patterns.name: Rock: four on the floor
patterns.note: Kick on every beat under the backbeat. On the chip the DMC kick has to retrigger four times a bar, which is cheap because the DMC is its own channel.

patterns.name: Rock: open hat on the and of 4
patterns.note: A lower period at the end of the bar. The renderer decays each hit over its own length, so a long note at period 10 gives the wash.

patterns.name: Rock: kick doubles the and of 2
patterns.note: The extra kick on the and of 2 is the classic rock syncopation. It costs one DMC hit and changes the whole feel of the bar.

patterns.name: Rock: pull back, kick on the and of 3
patterns.note: Kick lands late instead of early. A late kick drags, an early kick pushes; alternating the two across four bars is the cheapest groove writing there is.

patterns.name: Rock: tom groove
patterns.note: The hat lane is replaced by a tom at period 9. One channel, one note, and the bar sounds like a different kit.

patterns.name: Rock: crash on the downbeat, sparse bar
patterns.note: A long noise decay at period 12 under the kick reads as a cymbal crash. Use it on the first bar of a new section only.

patterns.name: Rock: double kick sixteenths
patterns.note: Kick on every eighth with the offbeat softer. On the NES this is one DMC retrigger per eighth, which is at the edge of what an 8 bit sample can do without a seam.

patterns.name: Rock: verse groove with dropped hat
patterns.note: Offbeat hats only, which is the standard reggae inheritance in rock. The bar breathes, and the chorus can sound bigger by comparison.

patterns.name: Rock: chorus groove, pedal hat
patterns.note: Quarter note hats at level 5. Fewer hits and more level than the verse, which is how a chorus gets louder without a louder kick.

patterns.name: Rock: stop time bar
patterns.note: Three hits in a bar of sixteen steps. Stop time is silence plus position, and the chip does silence better than anything.

patterns.name: Rock: shuffle eighths
patterns.note: The hat sits on the last sixteenth of each pair, which is the chip legal way to write a swung eighth on a straight grid.

patterns.name: Rock: tom pickup into the next bar
patterns.note: Two tom hits at the end of the bar. This is the smallest possible fill and the one an arranger will need most often.

patterns.name: Rock: rigid grid, deliberately flat (anti example)
patterns.note: Every hit the same level and the same position, which is the mechanical sound the ear review scored 3 out of 10. Kept as the control case for the humanising pass (DR-S07).

patterns.name: Metal: sixteenth double kick
patterns.note: At 150 to 190 bpm a sixteenth kick is the wall the feel needs. The accents on beats keep the bar legible inside the wall.

patterns.name: Metal: gallop (eighth plus two sixteenths)
patterns.note: One long then two short is the iron maiden gallop, and it is a kick pattern rather than a melody pattern here.

patterns.name: Metal: blast beat
patterns.note: Kick and snare alternate sixteenths. The chip can do this because the snare is noise and the kick is DMC, two separate channels, so nothing is stolen.

patterns.name: Metal: half time crush
patterns.note: Slow the backbeat to 8 and fill the gap with kicks. Half time plus displaced kicks is the standard heavy riff accompaniment.

patterns.name: Metal: kick on 1 and the and of 2, snare 3 and 4
patterns.note: Backbeat on 4 only, with a hit on 3 as well. The drums leave beat 2 empty for the riff to fill.

patterns.name: Metal: sixteenth kick with tom answer
patterns.note: Wall ends two steps early so the toms can answer. Dropping two kicks is enough to make a fill audible without a fill bar.

patterns.name: Metal: 6/8 gallop
patterns.note: The gallop sits naturally in 6/8: one long two short is the compound grouping already, so the drums state the metre instead of fighting it.

patterns.name: Metal: snare on every beat (tribal)
patterns.note: Snare on all four beats with the kick doubling 1 and 3. Reads as a war drum rather than a kit.

patterns.name: Metal: kick only, riff carries the downbeat
patterns.note: No snare for a whole bar. In metal the riff is the rhythm; a bar without snare makes the guitar sound twice as heavy.

patterns.name: Metal: blast with cymbal wash
patterns.note: The blast with one long low noise hit under it at the top of the bar. Period 13 is a rumble rather than a cymbal, which is the closest the chip gets to a ride wash.

patterns.name: Metal: half time with double kick under
patterns.note: The wall continues while the snare marks only beat 3, so the bar feels twice as long as it is.

patterns.name: Metal: stop, then two sixteenth kicks
patterns.note: Almost nothing: one hat, two kicks, one snare. Silence is the heaviest drum the chip has.

patterns.name: Baroque: timpani on the tonic
patterns.note: Two strokes a bar, nothing else. In a baroque texture the drums mark the metre and the continuo does the moving.

patterns.name: Baroque: two timpani pitches
patterns.note: Rate 10 and rate 12 give the tonic and the fifth from one DMC sample. Two rates are cheaper than two samples and sound like two kettledrums.

patterns.name: Baroque: menuet pulse
patterns.note: A menuet is a three step dance at moderate tempo. The drums mark 1 and 3, which is the weight the dance actually has.

patterns.name: Baroque: courante running accents
patterns.note: The courante is the fast three step dance; accents every third step is the running figure written as percussion.

patterns.name: Baroque: gigue in 6/8
patterns.note: Gigue is the compound metre dance of the suite, and its pulse is the dotted quarter, so the drums land on 0 and 6 and nowhere else.

patterns.name: Baroque: cadential hemiola in four
patterns.note: Three accents across four beats: the baroque hemiola in a single bar, which is what a cadence sounds like when the metre is being pulled to a stop.

patterns.name: Baroque: chaconne ground
patterns.note: One heavy stroke per bar over a repeating bass figure. The drums must not compete with the ground, so everything else is at level 2.

patterns.name: Baroque: concerto tutti accent
patterns.note: Kick and snare together only on the structural accents, the way a concerto orchestra hits with the tutti rather than continuously.

patterns.name: Baroque: siciliana in 6/8
patterns.note: The siciliana lilt lives in the dotted rhythm of the melody, so the percussion states only the two big beats per bar.

patterns.name: Baroque: timpani roll crescendo
patterns.note: A roll that grows one level every two steps. Timpani rolls are the one baroque drum gesture that needs no harmony to make sense.

patterns.name: Baroque: dance accent only on 1
patterns.note: One stroke and one breath. This is the maximum sparseness the ladder allows and it is where a harpsichord continuo wants the drums.

patterns.name: Baroque: toccata sixteenths
patterns.note: Sixteenth background at level 2 under three even snare taps. The density comes from the melody, so the drums stay at the floor.

patterns.name: Boss: half time menace
patterns.note: Slow backbeat and one displaced kick. A boss theme in a minor key wants the drums to sound like a heartbeat that skips.

patterns.name: Boss: tom pattern, low and slow
patterns.note: Two low tom answers per bar. On the noise channel the only pitch control is the period, so a tom pattern is a period pattern.

patterns.name: Boss: quarter note stomp
patterns.note: Every beat gets a kick, and the backbeat gets a snare on top. This is the march of an approaching boss.

patterns.name: Boss: triplet gesture on the backbeat
patterns.note: Two softer hits inside each backbeat read as a triplet at this tempo, and the uneven levels stop it sounding like a machine gun.

patterns.name: Boss: silence with two stabs
patterns.note: Three hits in a bar. A boss theme can carry almost no drums if the harmony is dissonant enough; this pattern is the proof.

patterns.name: Boss: snare roll into the next phrase
patterns.note: The last beat is a rising roll, so this pattern already ends with a section change built in.

patterns.name: Boss: 6/8 dirge
patterns.note: Compound metre makes the same groove sound older and slower. A boss that is ancient rather than fast wants 6/8.

patterns.name: Boss: kick pattern in threes against four
patterns.note: Kicks every three sixteenths inside a four beat bar. This is the cross rhythm the ear review asked for as odd tension, done in the drums rather than the harmony.

patterns.name: Boss: crescendo bar
patterns.note: Everything rises one level per beat. Use as the bar before a boss section change.

patterns.name: Boss: tom cascade at the end of the bar
patterns.note: Three tom hits with the period climbing 7, 9, 11, which is a falling pitch. A period sweep is the chip's pitch bend.

patterns.name: Boss: two bar pattern with a gap
patterns.note: The kicks never repeat within the bar. An asymmetric boss groove stops the player from predicting the next hit.

patterns.name: Boss: sixteenth floor under menace
patterns.note: Continuous sixteenth hat at level 3 turns a half time menace into a chase without moving the tempo.

patterns.name: Calm: brushed quarter pulse
patterns.note: A low period number is bright, so a calm brush uses a high one: period 7 at level 3 is a soft hiss, not a click.

patterns.name: Calm: rim ticks only
patterns.note: No kick at all. Three light snare ticks mark the phrase and leave the bar almost empty.

patterns.name: Calm: heartbeat kick
patterns.note: Two kicks close together then silence: a heartbeat rather than a beat. Good under a slow, sad cue.

patterns.name: Calm: 6/8 rocking pulse
patterns.note: One gentle kick per bar in compound metre. Anything more fights a lullaby melody.

patterns.name: Calm: noise swell
patterns.note: Period falls as the level rises, so the same hits get brighter and louder. This is a swell with no sample and no extra channel.

patterns.name: Calm: waltz for a memory
patterns.note: The plain waltz with every level halved. Same rhythm as WZ-01 and completely different mood, which is a point about level, not notes.

patterns.name: Calm: two strikes per two bars
patterns.note: Two hits in sixteen steps. Space is the instrument here; the arranger should let the melody carry the time.

patterns.name: Calm: soft noise floor with one accent
patterns.note: A quiet floor at period 8 with one darker, slightly louder hit at 8, which the ear hears as a shadow rather than a hit.

patterns.name: Battle: driving eighths, backbeat
patterns.note: The battle reference. Fast, eighths in the hat, backbeat on 2 and 4, nothing clever.

patterns.name: Battle: sixteenth kick with backbeat
patterns.note: Full sixteenth kick at the top end of the tempo range. The hat drops to quarters so the walls do not cancel each other.

patterns.name: Battle: snare roll every bar
patterns.note: A rising roll on beat 4 of every bar is too often, so use it for four bars then swap to BAT-01 for four. The pattern is written to make that swap easy.

patterns.name: Battle: tom answer
patterns.note: Same skeleton as BAT-01 with the last two steps given to the toms, so the eight bar phrase can end without a separate fill.

patterns.name: Battle: gallop
patterns.note: Two gallop cells a bar, which is the fastest way to make a B section sound like the same battle.

patterns.name: Battle: half time breathing bar
patterns.note: One half time bar inside a battle theme reads as a held breath. Put it at bar 8 of the phrase.

patterns.name: Battle: unison stomp
patterns.note: Kick and snare hit together on 1 and 3, which on the chip sounds like a much bigger kit than two channels.

patterns.name: Battle: 6/8 charge
patterns.note: A compound charge. The snare on the third eighth of each big beat is what makes 6/8 sound like galloping horses.

patterns.name: Battle: drop to rim before the loop
patterns.note: The bar before a loop point with almost nothing in it, so the loop start lands hard.

patterns.name: Battle: sixteenth snare crescendo fill
patterns.note: Half a bar of groove then half a bar of crescendo sixteenths. This is the single most useful battle bar in the file.

fills.name: One beat sixteenth roll, flat
fills.note: The plain roll. Four even hits, last one accented, kick underneath the first.

fills.name: One beat roll, crescendo
fills.note: Level rises 3, 5, 7, 9 across four steps. The single most useful fill in the file for a four or eight bar phrase.

fills.name: Two beat roll, crescendo
fills.note: Eight sixteenths rising from level 2 to level 9. Use at bar 8 and bar 16, not both in the same eight bars.

fills.name: Two beat roll, hairpin (loud to soft)
fills.note: A falling roll pulls the listener into the next phrase instead of pushing them. Use before a quiet section.

fills.name: One beat buzz roll in short mode
fills.note: Short loop mode gives the buzz the metallic edge that a straight noise roll lacks (DR-S01). The two lanes are the same chip channel, so the arranger must write them as alternating hits, not doubles.

fills.name: Roll with a gap before the downbeat
fills.note: The roll stops on the third beat, so the last two steps are silence and the next downbeat lands on nothing. A gap is a fill too.

fills.name: Roll that speeds up (eighths into sixteenths)
fills.note: Eighth, eighth, then sixteenths. The ear hears acceleration even though the grid never changes.

fills.name: Snare roll with a tom landing
fills.note: The roll hands over to two toms that drop in pitch, which is the fill a section change wants when the new section starts low.

fills.name: One beat tom drop, four hits
fills.note: Period climbs 6, 8, 10, 12, so the pitch falls. The noise period is the only pitch control on the channel, and a four step sweep is one beat at most tempos.

fills.name: Two beat tom drop, six hits then a kick
fills.note: Six toms falling into two kicks. This is the standard fill before a chorus or a boss phase.

fills.name: One beat tom rise
fills.note: The same sweep upwards. Rising toms sound like a question, falling toms sound like an answer; pick by what the next bar does.

fills.name: Two beat tom cascade, sixteen notes
fills.note: One continuous fall across two beats. The uneven levels (5, 6, 7 repeating) stop it sounding like a scale.

fills.name: One beat kick and tom alternation
fills.note: Kick, tom, kick, lower tom. Alternating the DMC and the noise channel is how the chip imitates a five piece kit with two channels.

fills.name: Two beat timpani style drop with roll
fills.note: Four strokes with the DMC rate falling, which is a timpani drop rather than a drum set fill. Rate is the DMC's pitch control, so a rate sweep is the sample's bend.

fills.name: One beat tom triplet gesture
fills.note: Three toms then a snare. On a sixteenth grid the triplet is a gesture rather than a true triplet, which is enough at any tempo above 100.

fills.name: Two beat tom sweep into a crash
fills.note: Four toms, then one very low noise hit at period 14 over a kick. The period 14 hit is the crash, and it needs a long note to decay.

fills.name: One beat closing flam
fills.note: Two hits one step apart, soft then loud, with a kick under the loud one. The cheapest fill that still reads as a fill.

fills.name: One beat flam cascade
fills.note: Two flams in a beat. The soft hit before each loud one is what makes a drum sound struck twice by a wrist rather than once by a machine.

fills.name: Two beat flams with ghosts
fills.note: Flam, ghost, flam, ghost. The ghosts are level 3 and they are what stop the fill from sounding like a metronome.

fills.name: Two beat flam into silence
fills.note: Two flams and then two beats of nothing. Silence before a new section is stronger than a louder fill.

fills.name: One beat flam on the downbeat
fills.note: A flam plus a low noise wash on the beat where the new section starts. The wash is what makes the flam sound large.

fills.name: Two beat flam and roll
fills.note: Flam to open the fill, crescendo roll to close it. This covers both jobs in the file with one gesture.

fills.name: One beat double flam
fills.note: A marching double stroke, written as two flams. The low noise hit on the last step gives it weight without a second sample.

fills.name: Two beat flam with tom answer
fills.note: Flam, gap, three falling toms into a kick. Use when the next section starts with a big harmony change.

fills.name: One beat crash with long decay
fills.note: One hit, low period, long note. A period of 14 gives the 2034 cycle rate, about 880 Hz of random clocking, which is the chip's rumble rather than its hiss (DR-S01). The decay is the note length, so hold it for a beat or more.

fills.name: Two beat crash swell
fills.note: Four long hits getting louder and darker. A ride wash written with one channel and no samples.

fills.name: One beat metallic crash (short mode)
fills.note: Short mode on a low period gives the metallic ring rather than a hiss, which is the closest the 2A03 gets to a china cymbal (DR-S01).

fills.name: Two beat cymbal choke
fills.note: A long hit at period 12 followed by a short bright hit at period 0, which reads as the cymbal being grabbed. The second hit must be short or the choke does not read.

fills.name: One beat crash into the downbeat
fills.note: Everything hits together one step before the new section, with the longest decay the chip has. The new section's downbeat then lands in the tail.

fills.name: Two beat cymbal and tom combination
fills.note: One long crash under three falling toms. Fills the two beats and still leaves the low end to the kick that follows.

fills.name: One beat kick and snare exchange
fills.note: Alternating kick and snare. Every drum in the kit speaks once, which is what makes a one beat fill feel finished.

fills.name: Two beat rock fill with open hat
fills.note: Kick, snare, kick, snare, with a long hat at the end. The open hat needs the following bar to start clean, so do not use it at a loop point.

fills.name: One beat waltz fill (4 steps in 3/4)
fills.note: One kick and three snare hits inside the last beat of a 3/4 bar. At 100 bpm a four step fill is 150 ms per hit, which is fast but playable.

fills.name: Two beat waltz fill (8 steps in 3/4)
fills.note: The last two beats of a waltz phrase filled. Because a 3/4 bar is twelve steps, eight steps is two beats and it will cross a bar line if the arranger is careless: place it on beats 2 and 3 only.

fills.name: Two beat march rudiment fill
fills.note: An uneven rudimental figure with the accents on 1 and the offbeat of 2. Marching snare fills are deliberately not even.

fills.name: Two beat battle crescendo fill
fills.note: Groove for a beat, then crescendo into the loudest hit in the library. Use once per loop at most.

fills.name: One beat drop out fill (silence)
fills.note: A single soft kick and three steps of nothing. The ladder's drop out rung applied to a fill: the absence is the gesture.

fills.name: Two beat boss fill with a low hit
fills.note: Ends on the deepest noise period there is. The period 15 hit is about a 4.7 Hz repeat, which reads as a sub thump rather than a cymbal.

fills.name: One beat unison hit and stop
fills.note: All three channels hit once on the last step. The chip's biggest single moment, and it costs three bytes of state.

fills.name: Two beat loop point turnaround
fills.note: Written for the two beats before a loop point: it ends soft, so the loop start is louder than the fill and the seam does not click. A loud fill at a loop point is what makes old game music sound like it stutters.

waltz_section.why: The ear review at 126 bpm (assets/audio/title_theme_v3/EAR_REVIEW_126.md) scored drums 4 of 10 and blamed a waltz pattern that never changes. This section is the answer: a family of waltz grooves plus a written rule set for varying them.

two_bar_hemiola_pairs.effect: three beats of 2/4 across two bars of 3/4
two_bar_hemiola_pairs.bars: any even bar pair after bar 3

two_bar_hemiola_pairs.effect: hemiola that resolves into a baroque cadence
two_bar_hemiola_pairs.bars: the two bars before a section change

two_bar_hemiola_pairs.effect: 6/8 heard as 3/4 then back to compound
two_bar_hemiola_pairs.bars: inside a 6/8 section, never at its start

rules.rule: Never run a waltz section on WZ-01 alone. The ear review of theme v3 scored drums 4 of 10 for exactly that, so WZ-01 is a control case here, not a groove.
Change one layer at a time: the kick position in bar 1, the ghost notes in bar 2, the snare weight in bar 3, and a fill in bar 4. Two layers moving in the same bar sounds like a different tune.
Establish three before playing two. A hemiola only reads when the listener has already heard a bar or two of plain waltz, so put WZ-02 and WZ-03 no earlier than the third bar of the section.
Hemiola is a two bar device. Pair WZ-02 (accent on 1 and 3) with WZ-03 (accent on 2) and never repeat one half alone; one bar of it reads as a mistake, two bars read as three beats against two.
The second kick goes on the and of 2 (step 6 of 12) or the and of 3 (step 10), never on beat 2 itself, which is the position the ear is already expecting as the weak beat.
Ghost notes stay at level 2 or 3 (velocity 28 to 42) and use a period of 5 to 7. A ghost at level 4 or louder stops being a ghost and becomes a second snare part.
One bar in every eight drops the kick entirely (WZ-28 or WZ-35). The silence costs no channel and it is the cheapest way to make the next bar sound composed.
A crash is a long note, not a loud one: period 12 to 14, level 7 to 8, held for a beat or more. Short hits at period 14 sound like a cough.
In 6/8 the snare belongs inside the big beat (steps 2, 3, 8, 9 of 12), not on it, because the dotted quarter already carries the accent.
Keep the level map stable inside a section: if the snare is level 9 in bar 1, it stays 9 unless the phrase is building. Changing levels at random is what the ear review heard as a rigid grid.

The bar before a section change takes a fill from the library, and the fill must end on or just before the downbeat of the new section. A fill that stops two steps early leaves a hole the new section has to fill.
Cut time in 3/4 (WZ-25 to WZ-27) is for a waltz that should feel slow without slowing down. Use it for one four bar stretch, then return to a three feel, or the metre stops reading as a waltz at all.

rungs.name: add ghost note
rungs.what: one soft hit at level 2 to 3 in an empty step

rungs.name: displace one accent
rungs.what: move the second kick to the and of 2 or the and of 3

rungs.name: add fill
rungs.what: the last beat or two beats of the bar becomes a fill from the library

rungs.name: drop out the kick for one bar
rungs.what: no DMC kick for a whole bar; the noise keeps the time

rungs.name: crash on the new downbeat
rungs.what: a long low noise hit on the first beat of the new section only

four_bar_cycle.bar_4: rung 3 with a one beat fill on the last beat
four_bar_cycle.note: The four bar cycle is the default. It changes the bar the listener remembers and leaves the home pattern in place for two thirds of the phrase.

eight_bar_cycle.bar_4: rung 3 with a one beat fill
eight_bar_cycle.bar_6: rung 1 plus a period sweep on the hat
eight_bar_cycle.bar_8: rung 3 with a two beat fill, ending the fill on the last step
eight_bar_cycle.note: The eight bar cycle adds the two devices a four bar phrase cannot hold: the displaced accent and the kick drop out. The last bar carries the bigger fill because eight bars is where a listener expects a seam.

sixteen_bar_cycle.what: two eight bar cycles, the second one starting with the crash rung and the section's other home pattern
sixteen_bar_cycle.note: The crash marks the top of the sixteen, so the phrase has a landmark without the drums getting busier.

hard_rules: Never climb two rungs in the same bar.
Never use rung 3 on two consecutive bars.
Rung 5 happens once per section, on the first bar only.
A section shorter than four bars gets rungs 0 and 3 and nothing else.

waltz_section.arranger_reading: Pick one home pattern per section from non_plain_3_4_ids (or pattern_ids_6_8 for a compound section), then read the variation ladder as a bar by bar script. WZ-01 stays unused except as a control.

fills_section.why: Forty fills, split by technique, each tagged with where it belongs so the arranger never has to invent one at bar 8.
placement_rules: phrase_end_4 means the last beat of every fourth bar; use a one beat fill, never two.
phrase_end_8 means the last beat of bar 4 and the last two beats of bar 8; the two beat fill is the bar 8 one.
phrase_end_16 means the last two beats of bar 16 or the last two beats before a loop point, and it is the one place a big fill is welcome.
before_section_change means the last beat before the new section starts, rising into the downbeat, and it may be used at 4, 8 or 16 depending on section length.
Never two fills in a row, and never a fill on the first bar of a section.

renderer_contract.note: How the arranger turns a hit into events for tools/render_chip.py (DR-S11).
renderer_contract.noise: MIDI note = period + 1, velocity = hit velocity, note length = the decay you want; for loop short send CC12 = 1 before the note.
renderer_contract.step_seconds: 60 / bpm / 4 for a 16th grid, 60 / bpm / 2 for the 6/8 eighth grid.
renderer_contract.one_sound_rule: The noise channel plays one hit at a time, so two noise hits written on the same step are an authoring error unless they are the same lane's alternation (DR-S08).
